"The first time I ever really listened to Kyle Kulinski’s show was in the back of a cab last summer. The driver had his phone hooked up through the stereo and was pumping out an episode through the car speakers — loudly, as if looking to convert a captive audience.

“Do you like Kyle Kulinski?”

The driver, Ahmed, was a recent immigrant and apparently a die-hard fan of Secular Talk, the political talk show that Kulinski broadcasts on YouTube. I told him, yes, in fact. I do like Kulinski, had come across his show several years ago, and, all things considered, he seemed pretty good.

“He understands what we’re up against,” Ahmed said. “Like Bernie.”

But I was surprised to hear Kulinski’s name mentioned in the same breath as Bernie Sanders, particularly with such adoration. Because what I did remember about Kulinski’s show struck me as mostly capital-P “progressive” takes on the news — the left wing of the Netroots crowd more than the democratic socialism Sanders has popularized.

It’s an impression that wasn’t entirely incorrect.

“I have no time for philosophical, airy bullshit,” Kulinski tells me from his home in Westchester, New York. “I don’t want to hear about Lenin. I don’t want to hear about Marx. I just want a super plainspoken, straightforward agenda with a straightforward way of selling it.”

With over 800,000 subscribers and nearly 670 million total views on YouTube, selling a progressive agenda is clearly something Kulinski knows how to do — even Democracy Now, the long-standing flagship of progressive media, cannot match his reach on the platform. Chapo Trap House can certainly boast a wildly devoted fan base (and a not insignificant degree of media influence), but their audience is roughly half the size of Kulinski’s.

While Secular Talk might be more likely to be looped in with the progressive networks around Air America and Pacifica alums like Sam Seder than the more resolutely socialist world, Kulinski’s fiery rhetoric, razor-sharp class instincts, and knack for withering takedowns sets him apart from his peers. Judging by his rhetoric alone, he’s closer to a Eugene Debs than a Chris Hayes.

But unlike Hayes, Amy Goodman, or his friend Cenk Uygur of The Young Turks — who began airing Secular Talk on his web network seven years ago — the thirty-two-year-old Kulinski is virtually invisible in the mainstream media. Despite his enormous fan base, his show has never once been mentioned in the obligatory trend pieces on “the Millennial Left” pumped out by the prestige media. Nor has Kulinski’s name ever popped up at all in the New York Times, Vox, the New Yorker, New York Magazine, or the Washington Post, despite his leading role in cofounding Justice Democrats, the organization widely credited with sweeping Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and the rest of “the Squad” to power.

Just last week, his Wikipedia page was deleted. The reason? “There is very simply no [reliable source] coverage of this person,” according to one moderator. In new media, he’s king — the Sean Hannity of the Berniecrat left. In old media, he’s nobody.

I suspect there are a few reasons for that. There is nothing “cool” about Kulinski’s show. (As a friend put it, “‘Welcome to Secular Talk’ sounds like something you’d hear on Egyptian radio.”) His no-nonsense social-democratic politics won’t get him much cred with the Full Communism crowd. He records his show not in Brooklyn or Los Angeles, but in a studio he built himself in his modest Westchester home. His hair is too groomed and his taste in clothes too preppy to qualify as “Dirtbag Left.” Nor has he ever attended an n+1 release party. “Not only have I not attended one,” he says, “I have no idea what that means.”

And yet he’s astonishingly plugged-in for a young man in the suburbs. Wondering how Sanders ended up on the Joe Rogan Experience? Kulinski, a frequent guest on Rogan’s wildly popular show, introduced them. “You make the most sense to me,” Rogan told Kulinski on a recent episode. “You’re a normal person.”

Much like Sanders himself, Kulinski’s show has a massive audience that just doesn’t compute with our media’s understanding of “what the kids want” or even “what the left-wing kids want.”

It’s probably for the best — the very woke and very WASP-ish decorum haunting much of the media world is nowhere to be found in Secular Talk. “Corporate Democrats over-focus on identity as a trick to divert you from the issues that unite us all — class issues,” he said on a recent episode.

A canard, in addition to being the French equivalent of "duck," is an unfounded rumor or story.  One such canard is the insistence that Ross Perot cost George H.W. Bush the 1992 presidential election.  To that, I say "quack" and present the following data.

Bill Clinton won four states worth 52 electoral votes (MD, NY, AR, DC) by a margin greater than Perot's share of the vote.  Bush won one state worth 7 EVs (MS) by a margin greater than Perot's share.  The remaining 46 states, worth 479 electoral votes, were decided by a margin less than Perot's share.  For the purpose of this discussion, we can ignore the seventeen states worth 161 EVs (NE, SC, UT, AL, ND, ID, OK, AK, VA, IN, WY, KS, SD, TX, FL, AZ, NC) won by Bush, though it is possible that Perot's presence could have impacted some of these races as well.

That leaves 29 states, worth 318 EVs, won by Clinton by a margin less than Perot's share of the vote:

GA - 13 EV - Clinton by 0.59 - Perot 13.34 - Bush needed 52.2
NH - 4 EV - Clinton by 1.22 - Perot 22.56 - Bush needed 52.7
OH - 21 EV - Clinton by 1.83 - Perot 20.98 - Bush needed 54.4
MT - 3 EV - Clinton by 2.51 - Perot 26.11 - Bush needed 54.8
NV - 4 EV - Clinton by 2.63 - Perot 26.19 - Bush needed 55.0
NJ - 15 EV - Clinton by 2.37 - Perot 15.61 - Bush needed 57.6
CO - 8 EV - Clinton by 4.26 - Perot 23.32 - Bush needed 59.1
WI - 11 EV - Clinton by 4.35 - Perot 21.51 - Bush needed 60.1
KY - 8 EV - Clinton by 3.21 - Perot 13.66 - Bush needed 61.7
ME - 4 EV -Clinton by 8.38 - Perot 30.44 - Bush needed 63.8
CT - 8 EV -Clinton by 6.43 - Perot 21.58 - Bush needed 64.9

IA - 7 EV - Clinton by 6.01 - Perot 18.71 - Bush needed 66.1

MI - 18 EV - Clinton by 7.40 - Perot 19.30 - Bush needed 69.2
LA - 9 EV - Clinton by 4.61 - Perot 11.81 - Bush needed 69.5
DE - 3 EV - Clinton by 8.19 - Perot 20.44 - Bush needed 70.0
OR - 7 EV - Clinton by 9.95 - Perot 24.21 - Bush needed 70.6
TN - 11 EV - Clinton by 4.65 - Perot 10.09 - Bush needed 73.1
MO - 11 EV - Clinton by 10.15 - Perot 21.69 - Bush needed 73.4
WA - 11 EV - Clinton by 11.44 - Perot 23.68 - Bush needed 74.2
MN - 10 EV - Clinton by 11.63 - Perot 23.96 - Bush needed 74.3
PA - 23 EV - Clinton by 9.02 - Perot 18.20 - Bush needed 74.8
NM - 5 EV - Clinton by 8.56 - Perot 16.12 - Bush needed 76.5
CA - 54 EV - Clinton by 13.39 - Perot 20.63 - Bush needed 82.5
VT - 3 EV - Clinton by 15.70 - Perot 22.78 - Bush needed 84.5
RI - 4 EV - Clinton by 18.02 - Perot 23.16 - Bush needed 88.9
HI - 4 EV - Clinton by 11.40 - Perot 14.22 - Bush needed 90.1
MA - 12 EV - Clinton by 18.52 - Perot 22.80 - Bush needed 90.6
WV - 5 EV - Clinton by 13.02 - Perot 15.92 - Bush needed 90.9
IL - 22 EV -  Clinton by 14.24 - Perot 16.64 - Bush needed 92.8

The last column is the share of Perot's vote Bush would have needed to swing the state, assuming all Perot voters would have chosen either Bush or Clinton.  It is possible that these voters would have chosen another third-party candidate or not voted at all, which would have made Bush's task even more difficult because the number of votes needed (the numerator) would have remained the same while the number of votes available (the denominator) would have decreased. 

Assuming all states behaved similarly, Bush would have needed to win every state down through Iowa on the list above.  He would have needed 66.1 percent of the Perot vote - assuming all Perot voters chose either Bush or Clinton - to accomplish this feat.  And it wouldn't have happened because Perot was far too liberal on social issues (e.g., he was pro-choice) to appeal to a majority of Bush voters.  It is just as likely that Clinton would have taken NC, AZ, or FL - all of which went to Bush by less than 2 percent - in Perot's absence than Bush would have taken GA, NH, or OH.

Let's blast that canard out of the sky once and for all.  Perot did not cost Bush the 1992 election.

transcript: So, as you all know, we've had many Zorn backed candidates recently win, DSA candidates recently win, left-wing insurgent challenger candidates recently win. And this is a big deal, bro. This is a big deal. And what I have here is a great clip for you. This is Hassan laying out in very simple terms how mega is cooked against Democratic socialists because finally we're fighting political battles and ideological battles on our grounds. This is what we've always wanted for a very long time. Now it's actually happening. Let's see what he has to say. Here we go. >> For the first time ever you are seeing Republicans take a defensive posture because the Democrats have not had a vision in the affirmative. Right? Democrats for the last three, four decades, since the Reagan era especially, have decided to play the defensive role. They are always telling you who they are not, who they oppose. They're never telling you who they are and what they stand for. >> So, right off the jump here, 100% correct. The other part I would add to that is they bought into the logic and the mindset and the framework and the ideology of their opponents. Bill Clinton came along with the DLC, the Democratic Leadership Council. He said, "Look, we're going to take corporate money too now. We're not only going to take union money or lawyer money. We are going to take corporate money too now. And we are also going to represent the will of corporations." And so, you basically had Democrats officially sort of rebrand the party as half Republican. In fact, they had a term for it. It's called triangulation where you're saying, "I'm not with these crazy right-wingers, but I'm also not with these crazy left-wingers. I'm in the middle. I'm above it all. I triangulate. I'm like the reasonable middle ground that nobody can disagree with." This is how they framed it. And at the time it was very electorally successful in 1992 when Clinton came out on the scene. Now, it's a little complicated why he ended up winning that race. It's not as simple as he was like just a generational political talent. You had Ross Perot which helped spoil the election for the win. I don't know if he would have won if it wasn't for Ross Perot helping against George H. W. Bush, right? But, this ushered in the the era where every Democratic politician and leader said, "This is it. This is the answer forever. No more far-left stuff. No more new deal Democratic mindset, FDR style mindset where we believe in social democracy and we want to check the excesses of capitalism. Now, it's we are we are dyed-in-the-wool neoliberals. We're going to be half Republican and all we can offer you is tweaks around the edges. We're not going to do any big universal programs anymore and things of that nature. And when you're in that defensive posture and you always half agree with your opponents, you can't really make a forceful case. You can't really make a forceful case without buying into their premise over and over and over and over and over. And then now finally, from 1992 all the way till now, finally we're we're beginning to see the fever break and the actual left-wing candidates, the new deal type candidates, they are the ones who are winning. >> Now that we have a different crop of Democrats, Democratic socialists, who are coming out and saying, "This is what we are for. This is the idealism that we want to represent. These are the policies that we want to implement. We are fighting for the working class and that's precisely what we're going to do. That's the the agenda that we have. That's our focus." All of a sudden, the Republicans have to play defense against that. Instead of coming out and running the gamut on a litany of different culture war issues that they have seen tremendous success on and then have the Democratic Party in its entirety run against those culture war issues by conceding on a lot of the hysteria to say, "Oh, well, we're just going to be a little bit more we're going to be a little bit less vicious to trans people and that's why you should vote for us." Instead of doing that, now we're having that battle on our terms.
